article_title: Task Automation, Worker Augmentation: Opportunities for Career and Technical Education in the Heartland
citation: Jacobs, B. (2026, September). Task automation, worker augmentation: Opportunities for career and technical education in the heartland. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/317
title: Shared dataset combining the Anthropic Economic Index with Census BTOS employer adoption data
description: The three-part brief series draws on "a shared dataset combining Anthropic's AI exposure index with the U.S. Census Bureau's Business Trends and Outlook Survey (BTOS) employer adoption data." The AEI tracks how AI models are actually used on the job task by task, mapped to standard occupational classifications, while BTOS measures whether employers have actually adopted AI in their operations regardless of technical exposure. Together they let the brief distinguish task-level exposure from firm-level adoption.
requirements: Both sources are needed because task-level exposure to AI and firm-level adoption of AI are not the same thing
constraints: BTOS excludes farm businesses from its sample entirely and underrepresents small employers
target_learners: Policymakers, funders, and CTE practitioners using labor-market data for program planning
target_learning_goals: Translating labor-market data on AI into actionable next steps for CTE
examples: The brief uses the two datasets to triangulate that both exposure and adoption remain low for Heartland-heavy occupations
key_sources: Jacobs, B. (2026, September). Task automation, worker augmentation: Opportunities for career and technical education in the heartland. Digital Promise. https://doi.org/10.51388/20.500.12265/317

article_title: Automated software scoring of senior school certificate examination mathematical items in economics using a contextual similarity model
citation: Olaoye DD, Owolabi HO and Olaoye OT (2026). Automated software scoring of senior school certificate examination mathematical items in economics using a contextual similarity model. Front. Educ. 11:1669504. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1669504
title: Automated Extended Essay Grading Software (AEEGS)
description: AEEGS is an AI-based web application developed by the researchers to score extended mathematical essay responses in senior secondary Economics without manual training on many model answers. It uses "contextual similarity, which is a pre-trained scoring algorithm used in this study in awarding scores to students extended essay responses which return index of 0–1", multiplied by the marks allotted in the marking scheme. It was built with HTML, CSS, MYSQL, PHP, Laravel, Python and FastAPIs on the waterfall model, and includes a candidate login interface, test-item interface and an online database of responses and scores.
requirements: The examiner must supply both the question items and the expected model answer (marking scheme) against which student responses are matched
constraints: Validated only on two Economics mathematical items; the article states the scores of other pieces of software were not correlated with it
target_learners: Senior secondary school III students studying Economics in South-west Nigeria
target_learning_goals: Scoring mathematical, graphical and computational Economics extended essay items at senior secondary certificate examination level
examples: Used to score 1,008 students' responses to Economics Paper II Section A mathematical items, with scores displayed in an online database backend
key_sources: Olaoye DD, Owolabi HO and Olaoye OT (2026). Automated software scoring of senior school certificate examination mathematical items in economics using a contextual similarity model. Front. Educ. 11:1669504. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1669504

article_title: 'A Systematic Review of Educators'' Engagement with AI in Problem-Based Learning'
citation: MOHAMMAD ANIQ AMDAN, AMDAN ASIM, NUR FIRZANA ROSMAN, NALDO JANIUS, FAIZUL HAFIZZIE DASUKI, NICHOLAS KAMARAU JOHNNY. (2026). A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF EDUCATORS’ ENGAGEMENT WITH AI IN PROBLEM-BASED LEARNING. Quantum Journal of Social Sciences and Humanities, 7(1), 1-14. https://doi.org/10.55197/qjssh.v7i1.787
title: AI-Enhanced Academic Interaction Model (AEAIM)
description: The review proposes the AI-Enhanced Academic Interaction Model (AEAIM), an integrative adoption framework that explains educators' adoption and use of AI-enhanced PBL. It integrates three theoretical bases: the Technology Acceptance Model, Constructivist Learning Theory, and Krashen's Input Hypothesis. The article states it "proposes the AI-Enhanced Academic Interaction Model (AEAIM), integrating the Technology Acceptance Model, Constructivist Learning Theory, and Krashen's Input Hypothesis to explain educators' adoption and use of AI-enhanced PBL." It is offered as the review's theoretical contribution toward sustainable AI integration in education.
requirements: Grounded in the three integrated theories: Technology Acceptance Model, Constructivist Learning Theory, and Krashen's Input Hypothesis
constraints: Proposed by the review as a framework; the article reports no direct empirical test of the model
target_learning_goals: educator adoption and use of AI-driven PBL tools
key_sources: MOHAMMAD ANIQ AMDAN, AMDAN ASIM, NUR FIRZANA ROSMAN, NALDO JANIUS, FAIZUL HAFIZZIE DASUKI, NICHOLAS KAMARAU JOHNNY. (2026). A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF EDUCATORS’ ENGAGEMENT WITH AI IN PROBLEM-BASED LEARNING. Quantum Journal of Social Sciences and Humanities, 7(1), 1-14. https://doi.org/10.55197/qjssh.v7i1.787

article_title: Feedback sources in essay writing: peer-generated or AI-generated feedback?
citation: Banihashem, S. K., Taghizadeh Kerman, N., Noroozi, O., Moon, J., & Drachsler, H. (2024). Feedback sources in essay writing: peer-generated or AI-generated feedback? International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-024-00455-4
title: Argumentative Essay Writing online module with FeedbackFruits peer feedback
description: An online module called "Argumentative Essay Writing" (AEW) delivered in Brightspace over two weeks, designed to improve students' essay writing skills through peer feedback. It uses the FeedbackFruits app embedded in Brightspace, whose peer feedback feature "empowers teachers to design tasks that enable students to offer feedback to their peers". In phase one students wrote essays individually; in phase two students were randomly invited to provide written asynchronous feedback on peers' essays.
requirements: Brightspace platform with the FeedbackFruits app integrated
a structured feedback prompt specifying word count and evaluation criteria
constraints: The study used it with 74 graduate food-science students at a single Dutch institution, so findings may be context-specific
examples: Students provided feedback between 250 and 350 words following a prompt about how the peer presented, elaborated and justified elements of an argumentative essay
key_sources: Banihashem, S. K., Taghizadeh Kerman, N., Noroozi, O., Moon, J., & Drachsler, H. (2024). Feedback sources in essay writing: peer-generated or AI-generated feedback? International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s41239-024-00455-4

article_title: How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language
citation: Palladino, P., Trotta, E., Bonvino, A., Carlucci, L., & Cottini, M. (2025). How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09414-4
title: AEQ-ES adapted to English as L2 for primary school children
description: An adaptation of the Italian version of the Achievement Emotion Questionnaire–Elementary School (AEQ-ES; Lichtenfeld et al., 2012; Raccanello et al., 2019) assessing enjoyment, anxiety and boredom toward learning English as L2 across lessons, homework and tests. The questionnaire "is composed of a series of 32 statements with responses on a Likert scale ranging from 1 (not at all) to 5 (very much)", accompanied by gender-adapted faces. Only mathematics-domain terms were replaced with English-language terms, preserving the original item structure; the adapted scale showed an internal reliability of α = 0.78.
requirements: Items use faces representing emotional intensity and children answer individually in class, with experimenter help available for items they do not understand.
constraints: Reliability of the original Italian mathematics version ranged between 0.61 and 0.93 in Omega values; the English adaptation was validated only in this study's sample.
target_learning_goals: measuring achievement emotions (enjoyment, anxiety, boredom) related to learning English as a second language
examples: Administered collectively in classrooms with no time limit at T0 and T1 in the present study.
key_sources: Palladino, P., Trotta, E., Bonvino, A., Carlucci, L., & Cottini, M. (2025). How do you feel during English class? Emotions and metacognition in primary school children learning English as a second language. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09414-4

article_title: Emotion theory in education research practice: an interdisciplinary critical literature review
citation: Eliot, J. A. R., & Hirumi, A. (2019). Emotion theory in education research practice: an interdisciplinary critical literature review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-018-09642-3
title: Achievement Emotions Questionnaire (AEQ) and its derivative instruments
description: The AEQ is the self-report instrument paralleling academic emotion theory, operationalizing Pekrun's taxonomy of achievement, epistemic, and social emotions arranged around positive/negative, activity/outcome-focused, and activating/deactivating axes. The review notes it "has generated variants for use in different age groups, subject areas, and languages in addition to the original English." Studies using academic emotions as a research construct overwhelmingly adopt the AEQ or a derivative, making the instrument central to the review's critique of measurement practice in education research.
requirements: Requires self-report administration, most frequently as a posttest questionnaire, which the review argues captures memories of emotions rather than real-time emotional states during instruction
constraints: The review questions its validity as a sole instrument, especially for adolescent subjects whose self-concept is developmentally fluid
target_learners: secondary school students in online courses
target_learning_goals: measuring academic emotions as variables in research on emotion and learning
examples: The Pekrun et al. (2011) validation study used a convenience sample of N = 389 undergraduates volunteering for extra credit, relying predominantly on structural equation modeling
key_sources: Eliot, J. A. R., & Hirumi, A. (2019). Emotion theory in education research practice: an interdisciplinary critical literature review. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-018-09642-3

article_title: Towards patient-centered healthcare: a scoping review of soft skills training in medical schools.
citation: Zagalo Daniela Mariana, Palmieri Cristiana, Resende Noelle, Costa Teresa, de Sousa Rute Dinis, Canhão Helena, Bozza Fernando A. (2026). Towards patient-centered healthcare: a scoping review of soft skills training in medical schools. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09059-0
title: AETCOM (Attitude, Ethics, and Communication) module for integrating communication skills into medical curricula
description: The AETCOM module is a structured curriculum module focusing on attitudes, ethics, and communication, cited by the review as an example of integrating communication skills into the teaching curriculum. The review reports that "This module has been well-received by medical students, with a significant majority of students reporting an improved understanding of sociocultural, ethical, and medico-legal aspects." Panel discussions and reflective exercises are noted as complementary andragogical approaches within communication skills teaching.
requirements: Integration into the teaching curriculum alongside panel discussions and reflective exercises
Faculty able to deliver structured attitude, ethics, and communication content
constraints: The review notes variable approaches to communication skills training make effectiveness difficult to evaluate
examples: The review cites the module as well received, with students reporting improved understanding of sociocultural, ethical, and medico-legal aspects
key_sources: Zagalo Daniela Mariana, Palmieri Cristiana, Resende Noelle, Costa Teresa, de Sousa Rute Dinis, Canhão Helena, Bozza Fernando A. (2026). Towards patient-centered healthcare: a scoping review of soft skills training in medical schools. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09059-0

article_title: The Power of Graphic Organizers: Effects on Students' Word-Learning and Achievement Emotions in Social Studies
citation: İlter, İ. (2016). The Power of Graphic Organizers: Effects on Students' Word-Learning and Achievement Emotions in Social Studies. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 41(1). http://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajte/vol41/iss1/3
title: Achievement Emotions Questionnaire (AEQ) short version adapted to Turkish social studies
description: The AEQ short version (Pekrun et al., 2011), based on Pekrun's control-value theory, was translated into Turkish and adapted to the social studies course to assess eight achievement emotions: enjoyment, hope, pride, anger, boredom, anxiety, hopelessness and shame. It uses a 5-point Likert scale and asks participants how they felt before, during and after the treatment. The adapted 30-item structure loaded on eight factors with reliability 82.14.
requirements: Back-translation by two experts for content-related item equivalence and expert review for aspect and content validity
constraints: Validated with 480 fourth-grade students in Bayburt elementary schools; subscale reliabilities ranged from α=.78 to α=.85
target_learning_goals: achievement emotions tied to vocabulary-learning activities and outcomes in social studies
examples: Administered before and after the 7-week vocabulary instruction treatment in both conditions
key_sources: İlter, İ. (2016). The Power of Graphic Organizers: Effects on Students' Word-Learning and Achievement Emotions in Social Studies. Australian Journal of Teacher Education, 41(1). http://ro.ecu.edu.au/ajte/vol41/iss1/3

article_title: The Effects of Multimedia and Learning Style on Student Achievement in Online Electronics Course
citation: Herman Dwi Surjono. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia and Learning Style on Student Achievement in Online Electronics Course. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Adaptive e-learning system (AES) for the Analogue Electronics course
description: An adaptive e-learning system developed for the undergraduate electronics course at Yogyakarta State University (Surjono, 2007a, 2007b). It presents learning material in one of four learning modes derived from student questionnaires, allows students to change their learning mode, and offers multimedia artefacts "in the form of film clips or animated schematics" via navigation buttons at the bottom of the learning material page. The course content covers a syllabus of 7 chapters learned over seven weeks with 2 hours access each week.
requirements: Students fill out questionnaires on first access so the system can assign a learning mode
constraints: Students have only limited on-line time during experimentation, which may prevent them from realizing they can change learning mode
target_learners: undergraduate students in the Department of Electronics at Yogyakarta State University
examples: In the experiment, the experimental group accessed the AES while the control group accessed a NON-AES with the same learning material, exercises and tests and a fixed sequential non-multimedia default.
key_sources: Herman Dwi Surjono. (2015). The Effects of Multimedia and Learning Style on Student Achievement in Online Electronics Course. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 14(1). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1057334

article_title: Effects of an Aesthetics-Based Educational Intervention on Compassion Competence and Aesthetic Care Quality Among Psychiatric Nurses: A Quasi-Experimental Study.
citation: Balideh Donya, Farokhzadian Jamileh, Miri Sakineh, Shahraki Sedigheh Khodabandeh, Motamed‐Jahromi Mohadeseh. (2026). Effects of an Aesthetics‐Based Educational Intervention on Compassion Competence and Aesthetic Care Quality Among Psychiatric Nurses: A Quasi‐Experimental Study. Nursing Open. https://doi.org/10.1002/nop2.70854
title: Four-session aesthetics-based nursing care training program for psychiatric nurses
description: A structured continuing-education program of "four structured 90‐min face‐to‐face sessions delivered once a week over four consecutive weeks", covering foundations of aesthetics-based care, psychological and spiritual dimensions, empathy and connectedness, and reflection on learning. Sessions used lectures, group discussions, educational videos, scenario analyses, and reflective assignments completed between sessions in groups of five, with content validated by a panel of seven experts and summarized in a booklet given to participants.
requirements: Delivery by trained facilitators (two nursing faculty members specializing in psychiatric nursing and aesthetics)
Content validated by an expert panel
Reflective assignments between sessions and group sharing of lived experiences
constraints: Evaluated only in a single psychiatric hospital with nurse-reported outcomes at a 1-month follow-up
target_learners: Psychiatric nurses with a bachelor's degree or higher and at least 6 months of psychiatric ward experience
target_learning_goals: Compassion competence including communication, sensitivity, and insight
examples: In the study, the intervention group received the four weekly sessions while the control group continued routine practice, with post-testing one month after program completion

article_title: Changing the landscape of medical anatomy education: impact of flipped classroom pedagogy on learning outcomes and perceptions of medical students in practical gastrointestinal anatomy.
citation: Mohammadi Shabnam, Mastour Haniye, Dadgar Moghadam Maliheh, Emadzadeh Ali. (2026). Changing the landscape of medical anatomy education: impact of flipped classroom pedagogy on learning outcomes and perceptions of medical students in practical gastrointestinal anatomy. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09522-y
title: Anatomy Education Environment Measurement Inventory (AEEMI)
description: The AEEMI is a validated, anatomy-specific instrument used to assess students' perceptions of the anatomy learning environment. It "consists of 108 items distributed across seven domains: perceptions of anatomy teachers, learning resources, learning atmosphere, student effort, content and organization, social self-perceptions, and overall satisfaction". Responses use a five-point Likert scale with higher scores indicating more favorable perceptions. In this study it demonstrated strong psychometric properties including test-retest ICC exceeding 0.80 and Cronbach's alpha of 0.80.
requirements: Expert panel evaluation for content validity using CVR and CVI indices
constraints: Scores are ordinal Likert-scale data, reported as medians
target_learning_goals: Assessing perceptions of the anatomy learning environment
examples: Used to compare learning environment perceptions between flipped and lecture-based groups in gastrointestinal anatomy
key_sources: Mohammadi Shabnam, Mastour Haniye, Dadgar Moghadam Maliheh, Emadzadeh Ali. (2026). Changing the landscape of medical anatomy education: impact of flipped classroom pedagogy on learning outcomes and perceptions of medical students in practical gastrointestinal anatomy. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-026-09522-y

article_title: Enhancing laparoscopic surgery training: a comparative study of traditional models and automated error detection system.
citation: Luo Yitian, Wang Jingjie, Yan Zongting, He Jingjing, Fu Liye, Wang Shenghan, Han Ying, Fu Yaoyu, Wang Xiandi, Li Kang, Yin Rong, Pu Dan. (2025). Enhancing laparoscopic surgery training: a comparative study of traditional models and automated error detection system. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07242-3
title: Automated Error Detection System (AEDS) for laparoscopic box training
description: AEDS is a hardware-plus-display add-on to a conventional laparoscopic ring-and-rail box trainer, with two components as the article defines them: "One is the automatic embedded contact device, which can collect the operator mistakes in training and record the corresponding number of errors", and an error feedback system adding an on-screen interface showing "the cumulative number of current operational errors as well as the total duration of the operation". After training, it exports tables of error times and a line-chart analysis. Error detection exploits the model's conductivity and binary circuit switching, enabling real-time mistouch feedback during practice.
requirements: Requires a conductive ring-and-rail training model wired to the contact device so mistouches register as circuit switches
Requires a display screen interface for real-time cumulative error and duration feedback
constraints: Errors are defined only as ring-to-rail contact, not excessive force, anatomical misidentification, or improper instrument manipulation
Evaluated only on the object-manipulation (picking up) skill module, not suturing or cutting
target_learners: novice undergraduate students with no prior laparoscopic training
target_learning_goals: laparoscopic object-transfer precision and error awareness
examples: Group A trained 10 min without AEDS then 10 min with AEDS activated; both assessments used AEDS for error detection
External differences between models with and without AEDS were kept minimal to reduce confounding from appearance
key_sources: Luo Yitian, Wang Jingjie, Yan Zongting, He Jingjing, Fu Liye, Wang Shenghan, Han Ying, Fu Yaoyu, Wang Xiandi, Li Kang, Yin Rong, Pu Dan. (2025). Enhancing laparoscopic surgery training: a comparative study of traditional models and automated error detection system. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07242-3
